title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from and where you live, state your nationality, and use regular verbs for the first three persons.
bekal: give your nationality in the right form
use -ar, -er and -ir verbs for *yo*, *tú* and *él / ella*

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En una fiesta
dialogs.intro: A party in Barcelona. Two people who haven't met yet make small talk.

notes: **Nationalities follow gender, and they're lowercase.** *indonesio* (male) / *indonesia* (female), *español* / *española*. Unlike English, nationalities do **not** take a capital letter — but country names do: *España*, *Indonesia*. The same goes for languages: *hablo español*, lowercase.

**The pattern is simple.** Adjectives ending in **-o** for men change to **-a** for women: *mexicano / mexicana*. Those ending in a consonant just add **-a**: *español / española*. Those ending in **-e** don't change at all: *estadounidense* works for both.

**-ar, -er, -ir verbs.** Every Spanish verb ends in one of these three. For "I", all three end in **-o**: *hablar* → *hablo*, *comer* → *como*, *vivir* → *vivo*. For "you", -ar becomes **-as** and the other two **-es**.
**De = from.** *Soy de Indonesia* = "I'm from Indonesia". Followed by *el*, the two merge into *del*: *del norte* (from the north), not *de el norte*. The same merge happens with *a + el* → *al*.
**¿En qué trabajas?** literally "in what do you work?" — the normal way to ask what someone does. The answer can be a place (*trabajo en una librería*) or a profession (*soy profesora*).
**Me gusta** means "I like", but it's built the other way around: literally "it pleases me". For now, learn it whole — the pattern is taken apart in Unit 13.
**Pero vs sino.** *Pero* = "but" in the ordinary sense. You'll meet *sino* later; it's used only after a negative sentence ("not this, but that").

**Pues** is an all-purpose linking word that's almost impossible to translate — "well", "then", "so", "because". Spaniards sprinkle it everywhere; you don't have to use it, but you do need to recognize it.

grammars.title: Regular verbs — the "I", "you", "he/she" forms
body: Drop the *-ar / -er / -ir* ending from the infinitive, then add the endings below. Once this pattern sticks, thousands of verbs open up at once:
after: Notice that **-er** and **-ir** differ only in forms you haven't learned yet (*comemos* vs *vivimos*, Unit 9). In these first three forms they're twins — so in practice you're memorizing **two** patterns, not three.

These three forms cover most one-on-one conversations: you talk about yourself (*yo*), about the person you're talking to (*tú*), or about someone you're both discussing (*él / ella*). The plural forms follow in Unit 9.

blocks.text: Three columns that are easy to mix up. Notice that the name of the language is always the same as the masculine nationality — once you know *japonés*, you automatically know the name of the language.
Notice the ´ disappearing in the feminine forms: *japonés* → *japonesa*, *francés* → *francesa*, *alemán* → *alemana*. The mark is no longer needed once the word gains a syllable.
